subtitle: Trace how rules, information and handoffs interact to create unequal outcomes, then identify a possible barrier and compare supported improvements.
scope: For staff examining service and workplace processes across DHS. A system here means connected rules, resources, tasks and decisions, not a computer product. Practice cases teach process inquiry without deciding eligibility, assigning motive or establishing legal findings. Actual changes, information use and required analysis follow authorized procedures.
introTranscript: Unequal outcomes can develop through a sequence of ordinary decisions rather than one obvious event. A requirement, a communication choice, a deadline and a handoff may interact in ways that are easier to see when staff examine the whole task. This course follows a practice service process in which people request a document, receive instructions and submit a response for review. You will map the steps, investigate a possible barrier, distinguish evidence from a causal claim, examine who can change the process and plan a responsible review. The purpose is to build practical inquiry, not to assume every difference has one cause or that staff can waive a requirement on their own.

lessons.title: See the connected process rather than one isolated step
lessons.summary: Map the sequence of a practice service task.
lessons.objective: Describe a system as connected rules, resources, tasks and decisions.
objectives: Describe a system as connected rules, resources, tasks and decisions.
Map a practice task from invitation through review.
Identify a boundary that keeps the inquiry focused and usable.
takeaways: Connected steps can create effects that one step alone does not explain.
A useful map identifies the actual task and its boundaries.
Mapping is an inquiry tool, not proof of a causal conclusion.
lessons.statement: Follow the task from the person’s starting point to the authorized decision.

image.caption: Four colleagues stand together in an open office and review a printed document.

intro.heading: A process is more than its written instruction
intro.body:
In this course, a system means connected rules, resources, tasks and decisions. A service request may involve an invitation, instructions, a supporting document, a submission route and a review. Each part can have a reasonable purpose while the sequence creates a difficulty that nobody sees when examining only their own step. Staff can investigate those connections without assuming that a particular colleague intended the result.

Consider a practice DHS service process. A person receives a notice, requests a document from another office, obtains the document, submits it through the service route and waits for review. The notice says when the response is due. The document office has its own turnaround, and the review unit uses a different name for the supporting document. Staff at each point may describe their own instructions as clear, yet the combined task may not be clear or feasible for the person using it.

Map the relevant sequence and identify what the inquiry includes. This course focuses on the request and review task, not every part of the person’s life or every policy in the agency. A focused boundary makes it easier to ask who has information, where a handoff occurs and which responsibilities matter. The boundary can be widened if appropriate evidence shows another relevant connection.

The map should distinguish a documented step from an assumption. A diagram can show how staff expect the process to work, but its arrows do not establish how it actually worked for everyone. Check instructions, authorized records and affected perspectives. Use practice information in the learning activity and keep actual protected records in their proper process. The result is a clearer question about the task, not a completed investigation or proof that one person caused an unequal outcome.

lessons.keyStatement: The map organizes inquiry; evidence shows what happened.

flashcards.back: Connected rules, resources, tasks and decisions that shape how work occurs.
A transfer of information or responsibility between steps or people.
The part of the work being examined and the relevant connections it includes.
How the process is expected to work, which may differ from actual use.

items.title: Starting point
items.body: Begin where the person learns that a response is needed. A staff-only map starting at receipt can miss the work required to obtain a document. Including that preparation helps identify which instruction and timing questions belong in the review.

items.title: Connections
items.body: Name what passes between offices and what each step depends on. The service review may depend on a document with a different name in another office. This connection is a question to examine, not evidence that either office is careless.

items.title: Boundary
items.body: Limit the first inquiry to a task that can be understood. Do not gather every personal circumstance in case it becomes useful. Broaden the boundary only when the question and authorized evidence justify it, and explain what remains outside the inquiry.

tabs.heading: Three ways to view the process

tabs.label: One instruction
tabs.body: The notice may be accurate as a document but does not show how its deadline interacts with another office’s turnaround. Review its place in the sequence instead of assuming its individual clarity settles the whole task.

tabs.label: Connected task
tabs.body: A task map shows dependencies and helps staff ask specific questions about timing and handoffs. Verify the sequence with appropriate evidence and perspectives; a neat diagram is not proof that the process works.

tabs.label: Unlimited inquiry
tabs.body: An unlimited inquiry can overwhelm staff and collect unnecessary information. Choose a clear question and boundary so the next evidence and responsibility are understandable. A focused inquiry can expand later if needed.

check.question: What does the practice task map establish?
check.correct: The expected sequence and dependencies to investigate, with actual use and causal conclusions still needing evidence.
wrong: The identity of the person who caused every problem.
Proof that the written process works for everyone.
Authority to change every connected requirement.
check.feedbackCorrect: The map is useful because it identifies questions, while evidence and authority remain separate.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A diagram cannot establish personal motive, universal usability or decision authority. Name the steps and dependencies, then identify the appropriate evidence and responsible review for the particular task.

items.text: Request the supporting document.
Submit the response for review.
The notice deadline depends on the document turnaround.
Two offices use different names for the same practice document.
A diagram proves the process is equitable.
The map authorizes every policy change.

lessons.next: Next, examine how a possible barrier can build across the linked steps.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Each office reviews its own instruction and declares the full service task usable without checking the other steps.
options: Map the task and examine the dependencies with appropriate evidence.
Assign blame to the last office in the sequence.
Collect every personal record before choosing a question.
responses: This reveals the connections that an isolated review can miss.
The last step does not establish who or what caused the problem.
The collection exceeds a focused inquiry and may create privacy problems.

lessons.transfer: Map the practice task as starting point, steps, handoffs, expected result and an evidence question.

move.control: You can describe a focused process and its dependencies.
move.failure: A review of one instruction is mistaken for a review of the whole task.
move.next: Map the practice request sequence and identify one connection to investigate.

lessons.title: Trace how a burden can accumulate
lessons.summary: Develop a testable explanation of a possible process barrier.
lessons.objective: Locate a dependency that may create an added burden.
objectives: Locate a dependency that may create an added burden.
Distinguish a plausible mechanism from an established cause.
Identify a feasible evidence question about the task.
takeaways: A barrier can build through timing, language and handoffs.
A plausible explanation still needs evidence.
Do not turn a process question into a group stereotype.
lessons.statement: Explain the possible connection step by step and test it.

image.caption: Four colleagues stand together in an open office and review a printed document.

intro.heading: A sequence can matter even when no single step looks extreme
intro.body:
A process burden can accumulate when several demands interact. An instruction may use an unfamiliar document name, a request office may need time to respond, and a submission route may require another visit. Each demand changes the practical task. A staff member should describe the possible connection rather than assume that every person experiences the same burden or that a difficulty comes from an identity trait.

In the practice case, the notice calls the document a verification summary while the request office calls it a confirmation letter. A person asks for the first name and receives no clear match. After clarification, the document is requested, but less time remains before the service response is due. The team can examine whether the naming difference led to confusion and delayed the task. That account describes a possible mechanism: how one step may affect the next.

The explanation is not established merely because it sounds reasonable. Other conditions may matter, such as when the notice arrived, whether the person needed language assistance, whether the document was already available or which response route was used. Ask what appropriate evidence supports each link and what alternative explanation remains plausible. One account can reveal a concern without establishing its frequency.

The team may be able to clarify the document name within its role, while a deadline or eligibility rule requires another authority. Do not promise a waiver or call the person unmotivated because the sequence was not completed. Identify the actual burden, the evidence needed and the responsible review. This approach keeps the task concrete and makes it possible to compare proportionate responses instead of relying on a broad claim that the system is simply good or bad.

inThisLesson: Trace its possible effect on timing.
lessons.keyStatement: A plausible mechanism is a question to test, not a finding to announce.

flashcards.back: A proposed explanation of how one condition affects another.
Added task demands that develop across connected steps.
Another plausible account that should be examined before settling on a cause.
A response connected to the actual issue, evidence and available authority.

items.title: Naming
items.body: Check what both offices call the document and how a person is directed to request it. If the names differ, the team can investigate whether the instructions explain that equivalence. The difference itself does not establish that every person was confused.

items.title: Timing
items.body: Trace the arrival, clarification, request and submission points in the practice task. That can identify which delay matters. Actual records require authorized access and proper interpretation; an approximate recollection should be described as such rather than reported as an exact timeline.

items.title: Other conditions
items.body: Ask which conditions could also affect completion. A person might already hold the document or use another permitted route. Recognizing these variations improves the explanation without dismissing the concern or treating every missed response as a personal failure.

tabs.label: Personal blame
tabs.body: Calling the person careless skips the connected naming and timing questions. Examine the task and supporting account before making a relevant conclusion. Identity or a missed step cannot establish motivation.

tabs.label: Plausible process explanation
tabs.body: The naming mismatch may have added clarification work and shortened the response window. Test the links through appropriate evidence and perspectives. State the limits, including whether this happened beyond the described case.

tabs.label: One cause for everything
tabs.body: The naming issue may matter without explaining every result. Other barriers can occur at different steps. Keep the inquiry open to alternative evidence instead of treating the first plausible story as a complete diagnosis.

check.question: Which statement treats the naming issue appropriately?
check.correct: It may create confusion and delay; the links, other conditions and extent need evidence.
wrong: It proves the reason for every late response.
It proves the person lacked interest.
It authorizes an immediate change to every deadline.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement explains a testable mechanism while keeping cause, extent and authority separate.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A plausible naming barrier cannot establish every outcome or motive. It also does not create authority to waive a requirement. Trace the task, test the links and identify the appropriate response process.

items.text: Different names may add clarification before a request.
A delayed clarification may leave less submission time.
Do the instructions explain both document names?
What other conditions affected the described timeline?
The first explanation proves every late response.
Group identity explains willingness to complete the task.

lessons.next: Next, interpret unequal results with suitable evidence and context.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A naming mismatch plausibly delayed one response, and staff want to announce it as the cause of all missed deadlines.
options: A bounded possible explanation and an appropriate plan to test its links and extent.
A different personal motive assigned to the person.
A declaration that the concern is irrelevant because only one account is known.
responses: The account is useful without being treated as a universal finding.
A new motive claim would still lack evidence.
One account can identify an important question while its extent remains unknown.

lessons.transfer: Write the possible naming-to-delay mechanism, one alternative explanation and an evidence question.

move.control: You can make a process explanation testable.
move.failure: A reasonable story becomes a universal cause without supporting evidence.
move.next: Trace the practice burden and identify what would support or challenge the explanation.

lessons.title: Interpret unequal results without guessing their cause
lessons.summary: Assess whether evidence supports the comparison and the claim being made.
lessons.objective: Distinguish process evidence from a broader outcome measure.
objectives: Distinguish process evidence from a broader outcome measure.
Identify comparability and missing-information limits in a practice table.
State a supported difference without an automatic inequity or cause finding.
takeaways: The evidence must match the question.
Different periods, definitions or missing records can weaken a comparison.
Group patterns do not explain each individual or establish their own cause.
lessons.statement: Describe the result and its limits before choosing an explanation.

image.caption: Four colleagues stand together in an open office and review a printed document.

intro.heading: A table is part of the inquiry
intro.body:
A team may use evidence to examine whether the task works differently across groups or settings. First identify the question. Did the instruction reach people, did the document arrive, did the response reach the person responsible or did the intended service result occur? These are different stages. A figure describing one stage should not be presented as proof of another.

In a practice table, Unit A records completed responses for one month while Unit B records them for three months. The team cannot compare the totals as if the periods and opportunities were identical. Even comparable completion rates would need definitions, suitable denominators and context before a wider conclusion. A pattern can prompt examination of a burden without establishing that the burden caused it.

DHS’s policy distinctions concerning inequities and disparities involve more than any arithmetic difference. Staff should preserve the actual meaning of a formal claim and identify the evidence needed to support it. Do not attach a group label to an assumed lack of effort, or infer an individual experience from the average. Missing information also cannot be counted as success or used to declare no concerns.

For actual data, use the authorized purpose, access and sharing process. Check definitions, periods, missing values, overlap, small groups and privacy protections with the person responsible. Removing names does not make every table safe to share. Where comparison is not supportable, report the information gap and the next appropriate inquiry. A useful analysis can state a bounded result and uncertainty. It should not manufacture a fairness score or a causal finding because the team would prefer a simple answer.

lessons.keyStatement: The strength of the claim depends on the evidence, not the display’s precision.

flashcards.back: Evidence about how a task or step was carried out.
Evidence about the intended result rather than the activity alone.
Whether definitions, periods, denominators and relevant conditions support a meaningful comparison.
A conclusion stronger than the evidence and design can establish.

items.title: Stage
items.body: An instruction sent is activity evidence. A complete response reaching the person responsible is a different result. Neither alone establishes the person received the intended service benefit. Choose the measure for the question and avoid substituting an easy count for the real inquiry.

items.title: Comparable records
items.body: Check the practice one-month and three-month periods before interpreting totals. A common column heading does not make the records comparable. If the comparison cannot be repaired with appropriate evidence, explain the gap instead of averaging it away.

items.title: Safe interpretation
items.body: A group-level pattern may identify a concern while individual circumstances vary. Ask which evidence supports a mechanism and use proper privacy protections. Do not rank employees, service users or communities by an invented score or share small-group details casually.

tabs.label: Raw totals
tabs.body: Totals can describe the recorded periods but may be misleading when presented as equal opportunity. State the period and definition clearly. The team needs a comparable basis before calling one process more effective.

tabs.label: Bounded comparison
tabs.body: A bounded comparison explains the suitable records, what differs and what remains unknown. It can identify a next process question without making the group itself a causal explanation.

tabs.label: Automatic diagnosis
tabs.body: An automatic diagnosis treats the display as proof of motive or cause. The table cannot supply those conclusions by itself. Combine the appropriate evidence, context and inquiry design rather than add a precise-looking label.

check.question: What should staff say about the different recording periods?
check.correct: The totals describe different periods and need a suitable comparison basis before interpreting a difference.
wrong: The larger total proves a fairer process.
A missing record means the task succeeded.
The unit name explains the cause.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement preserves the evidence limit and identifies the next data question.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Different periods cannot be ignored, missing information cannot be invented and a label cannot explain cause. State definitions and periods, obtain appropriate review and make the claim proportionate to the evidence.

items.text: Unit A’s count covers the practice one-month period.
The record describes responses received, not final service outcomes.
Unit B’s period differs and needs review before comparison.
A group difference does not establish an individual motive.
Missing information means there was no barrier.
A precise chart proves the mechanism.

lessons.next: Next, examine how decision authority and resources shape the process.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A chart ranks the units using totals from different periods and calls the smaller number evidence of employee indifference.
options: Remove the unsupported ranking, clarify the records and investigate the actual process question.
Use brighter colors to make the ranking more persuasive.
Treat uncertainty as proof that no inquiry is possible.
responses: This corrects the evidence claim and returns to a useful task inquiry.
Visual polish cannot supply comparability or explain motive.
A bounded inquiry can continue while evidence limits are stated.

lessons.transfer: Identify a practice measure, its period, a comparison limit and an authorized next evidence question.

move.control: You can match the evidence to the question and explain its limits.
move.failure: A convenient count becomes a causal or personal judgment.
move.next: Review the practice table before choosing a conclusion.

lessons.title: Examine who can decide and who carries the burden
lessons.summary: Connect a process concern to responsibility, influence and feasible action.
lessons.objective: Identify a decision point and the role with authority over it.
objectives: Identify a decision point and the role with authority over it.
Describe who may carry a proposed change’s burden.
Plan a contribution route that can inform the authorized decision.
takeaways: Power includes control of rules, information and practical choices.
Staff can identify an issue without holding every decision authority.
Affected input should inform a real choice, with accurate limits.
lessons.statement: Make responsibility and influence visible before promising a change.

image.caption: Four colleagues stand together in an open office and review a printed document.

intro.heading: A barrier review needs the right people and a real decision point
intro.body:
A process is shaped by who controls its rules, information, resources and decisions. Staff at the final review step may see a recurring difficulty but may not control the notice, the document office or the deadline. A useful inquiry identifies those responsibilities instead of assuming that one person can change the entire sequence.

In the practice case, the communication team can clarify the two document names, the document office can explain its expected turnaround and the service program controls the authorized submission rules. People using the process can describe what the combined task requires. Each contribution matters to a different question. The team should identify which choice is open, who can decide it and which requirements constrain it.

A proposed improvement can also shift work to someone else. A longer explanation may reduce confusion but require staff translation or document review. An assisted route may help some people while adding appointments or dependencies. Ask who carries that work and whether the person has the resources, authority and usable access to complete it. Do not treat senior agreement as proof that all affected people can deliver the plan.

Give affected perspectives an appropriate route into the decision while it can still be informed. Explain what the team can change, what must be referred and how the input was considered. Input may support an unchanged choice or identify an unresolved condition; it does not guarantee every preference will be adopted. The consultant can provide guidance and feedback, while staff and responsible offices retain their work and authority. Keep the process concrete and avoid substituting a consultant approval gate for the actual responsibilities that apply.

lessons.keyStatement: A supported concern and the authority to decide its response are different roles.

flashcards.back: The assigned role or process that can authorize a particular choice.
How relevant knowledge can inform a choice, including its reasons.
Time, staffing, information or other practical support needed to implement an option.
Added work or difficulty moved to another person or step by a proposed change.

items.title: Open choice
items.body: Identify whether the wording, submission method or timing is actually open for this review. A team can improve an instruction within its role while a rule change requires another office. A clear boundary allows useful work without an unauthorized promise.

items.title: Implementation burden
items.body: Trace what the proposed response asks others to do. If an assisted route requires appointments, investigate whether that creates another difficulty. A reasonable idea can fail when the necessary staff time or access is absent.

items.title: Input and reasons
items.body: Invite appropriate task knowledge before finalization and explain how it informed the decision. If a proposal is not adopted, give the reason and unresolved question. Do not ask a participant to represent everyone or treat continued disagreement as evidence of unwillingness.

tabs.label: One-person repair
tabs.body: A staff member may be able to clarify one step but cannot assume authority over every connected rule. Document the part within the role and coordinate the remaining responsibilities rather than promise an agencywide change.

tabs.label: Shared review
tabs.body: A shared review can bring task knowledge and decision authority together. It needs a clear question and a real choice, not a meeting that asks people to endorse a completed decision without influence.

tabs.label: Consultant permission gate
tabs.body: Consultant support can strengthen the inquiry but is not universal permission to use resources or raise a concern. Staff should keep their responsibility and follow the actual authorized processes. Do not replace those processes with a new approval requirement.

check.question: What should the team clarify before promising a new submission rule?
check.correct: Who has authority, which requirements apply and how affected knowledge and implementation burdens will be examined.
wrong: Whether everyone likes the proposed label.
Whether the consultant can approve every agency rule.
Whether extra work can be assigned without checking resources.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response connects the proposal to actual authority, evidence and feasible implementation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Agreement and labels do not create authority, and consultant guidance does not replace authorized offices. Trace the decision, constraints and work burden before making a promise.

items.text: Who can change the submission method?
Which requirement constrains a deadline decision?
Who would staff the assisted route?
Would another appointment create a new difficulty?
Can task input reach the decision before finalization?
How did an account inform an unchanged choice?

lessons.next: Next, compare proportionate changes to the connected task.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Staff promise to change the deadline without checking who controls it, and assign another office extra work without consultation.
options: Identify authority, requirements, resources and affected input before revising the proposal.
Keep the promise because changing it might be awkward.
Require consultant approval for every future staff question.
responses: This repairs the decision process rather than defending an unsupported promise.
The original promise cannot supply missing authority or feasibility.
A universal gate would not resolve the actual responsibilities.

lessons.transfer: Map a proposed change to decision authority, resource need, affected input and an unresolved condition.

move.control: You can identify responsibility and coordinate a supported proposal.
move.failure: A visible improvement is promised without authority or feasible implementation.
move.next: Clarify who can decide and who would carry the work.

lessons.title: Compare changes without reproducing the barrier
lessons.summary: Develop a proportionate response and check its full task path.
lessons.objective: Compare a wording repair, a handoff repair and a broader process proposal.
objectives: Compare a wording repair, a handoff repair and a broader process proposal.
Identify an unintended burden or excluded perspective in an option.
Write a conditional recommendation connected to evidence and authority.
takeaways: The response should fit the supported issue.
A local improvement can move a problem to another step.
Compare benefits, burdens, limits and implementation conditions.
lessons.statement: Check where the proposed repair leads next.

image.caption: Four colleagues stand together in an open office and review a printed document.

intro.heading: A change needs more than a plausible benefit
intro.body:
Once the task and authority are clearer, compare feasible responses. A small repair may be sufficient for one barrier, while a recurring connected problem may need a broader proposal. Staff should explain why an option fits the evidence and what it leaves unresolved rather than assume that the biggest change is always best.

In the practice case, the team considers naming the document consistently, adding a clear handoff explanation and proposing a review of the response timetable through the authorized program process. Consistent naming may reduce one confusion. The handoff explanation may clarify when the document is requested and how it reaches review. A timetable proposal may address another dependency but needs the appropriate requirements and decision authority. None of those choices should be presented as a guarantee that every person will complete the task.

Trace each option through the full sequence. A new instruction could be clear but inaccessible. An assisted route could receive a document but fail to deliver it to the person responsible. A proposed timing change could help one step while creating a conflict at another. Include appropriate perspectives and evidence so the team notices the new burden instead of celebrating the change’s appearance.

A conditional recommendation describes the preferred next action and what must be verified. For example, clarify both document names within the communication role, check the handoff with the document office and submit the remaining timetable question to the responsible program review. Record the evidence, limits and follow-through. A recommendation is useful when it makes the next decision clearer; it should not conceal an unresolved requirement or claim the task is equitable because an option received the highest informal score.

lessons.keyStatement: The repair must work through the task, not only at the point where it is introduced.

flashcards.back: A change to a particular step that addresses a supported issue.
A change affecting connected rules or responsibilities that needs appropriate authority.
A new difficulty created or shifted by a proposed response.
A proposal that states its evidence and the conditions needing verification or authorization.

items.title: Wording
items.body: Consistent naming can answer a clear communication issue. Check that the explanation is accurate, usable and reaches people when needed. It does not establish that another dependency, such as document turnaround, is resolved.

items.title: Handoff
items.body: A clearer handoff can explain where to request and submit the document. Verify what happens after submission. A route that loses information between offices may be easy to describe yet still ineffective in practice.

items.title: Broader review
items.body: A timetable question may require program or legal review, depending on the applicable rule. Frame the evidence and alternatives without promising an unauthorized exception. The scope of the proposal should follow the problem and responsibility, not the desire for a dramatic change.

tabs.label: Change the label only
tabs.body: A label change may help if the naming difference is the supported barrier. Check the actual instruction and remaining task conditions. A new name without an accurate explanation may simply move the confusion.

tabs.label: Repair the supported steps
tabs.body: This option clarifies naming and the handoff within the relevant roles while preserving unresolved timetable questions. Its benefit needs verification, but it can make appropriate progress without claiming everything is complete.

tabs.label: Declare a complete redesign
tabs.body: A redesign can be justified when evidence supports it, but cannot be assumed necessary or authorized. Compare resource needs and risks. A broad promise may hide the immediate repair the team can actually make.

check.question: Which recommendation is best supported by the practice inquiry?
check.correct: Clarify the supported naming and handoff issues within the relevant roles, and refer the remaining timetable question with evidence and limits.
wrong: Rename the process equitable and stop reviewing it.
Rank options using an unexplained precision score.
check.feedbackCorrect: The recommendation fits the supported issue, preserves actual responsibility and identifies what remains open.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A waiver, label or apparent precision cannot supply authority and evidence. Compare the full task, benefits, burdens and conditions, then identify a proportionate next action and responsible review.

items.text: Consistent document names may reduce clarification work.
A clear handoff may help the document reach review.
The revised instruction is accurate and usable.
The timetable proposal reaches the authorized decision maker.
A positive label proves the barrier is gone.
The highest unexplained score authorizes the choice.

lessons.next: Finally, examine whether the change worked and what the evidence can establish.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A new assisted route receives documents, but the team has not checked how they reach the service staff.
options: The full handoff, information handling, responsibility and remaining access conditions.
Only whether the route has a welcoming name.
Whether every person agrees the change is perfect.
responses: The option must work through the task, with appropriate safeguards and limits.
A name cannot establish a functioning handoff.
Universal agreement is not a practical verification method.

lessons.transfer: Write a conditional recommendation with benefit, burden, full handoff, authority and a remaining question.

move.control: You can compare proportionate options and explain their conditions.
move.failure: A repair moves the difficulty to another step while being reported as complete success.
move.next: Trace the proposed change through the practice task before recommending it.

lessons.title: Review the change without treating sequence as proof of cause
lessons.summary: Plan evidence of implementation, effect and remaining uncertainty.
lessons.objective: Distinguish implementation evidence from outcome and causal-impact questions.
objectives: Distinguish implementation evidence from outcome and causal-impact questions.
Identify an alternative explanation for a change after a repair.
Plan a responsible follow-up using a practice case or suitable draft.
takeaways: A change introduced is not necessarily a change that worked.
An outcome observed afterward does not establish sole cause.
Follow-through needs evidence, responsibility and appropriate limits.
lessons.statement: Check what changed, how the task worked and what remains unproven.

image.caption: Four colleagues stand together in an open office and review a printed document.

intro.heading: Review the result at the right level
intro.body:
A review should ask whether the proposed action occurred, whether it helped the intended task and what the evidence can establish. Those are related but different questions. CDC’s evaluation guidance distinguishes implementation, outcome and causal-impact inquiries. A before-and-after observation can describe a change but does not automatically establish that the repair caused it.

In the practice task, both offices now use the same document names, the revised notice explains the handoff and more responses reach review in the next recorded period. The naming and instruction changes are implementation evidence. The response result is relevant to an outcome question, but its explanation may also involve a changed invitation list, another time of year or staffing differences. Check suitable comparison evidence and context before attributing the result entirely to the repair.

Choose a focused review question and identify the role responsible for it. Verify the instruction and handoff, examine appropriate affected accounts and use authorized data with clear definitions and protections. A change in the average may still leave a barrier at another step or for some people. Missing information should remain visible; it cannot be treated as proof of no concern.

For actual DHS decisions, the required equity analysis and other applicable procedures remain separate from this learning exercise. The consultant can support interpretation and feedback without replacing staff work or authorized review. Practice with the practice sequence or a suitable draft within your role. Record a supported result, its limits and the next responsible action rather than declare the whole process equitable or demand completion of a live agency change. The aim is useful follow-through that can be refined as evidence develops.

lessons.keyStatement: Report the result at the level the evidence supports.

flashcards.back: Did the intended change occur and operate as planned?
Did the intended result occur, with definitions and limits stated?
What difference did the intervention cause relative to a credible alternative condition?
A responsible next action and a review of its actual use and effect.

items.title: Action carried out
items.body: Verify whether both document names and the handoff explanation changed in the actual material. A plan or meeting decision alone does not establish implementation. In the practice exercise, state which record would show the change without claiming a live agency repair occurred.

items.title: Task effect
items.body: Examine whether people could identify, obtain and submit the document through the revised task. Use appropriate perspectives and suitable records. A response count can be useful while failing to represent people never invited or another unresolved barrier.

items.title: Cause and next step
items.body: Consider other conditions that changed during the period. A better result after the repair does not settle attribution. State what the evidence supports, what remains uncertain and which inquiry would make the next decision clearer.

tabs.label: Activity only
tabs.body: “The notice was revised” identifies an action. It does not show that the handoff worked or an intended outcome occurred. Keep the action record and add the appropriate task review.

tabs.label: Bounded result
tabs.body: “The naming changed and recorded responses increased, but other conditions differ” states useful evidence with limits. It allows further inquiry without declaring sole cause or universal success.

tabs.label: Causal guarantee
tabs.body: “The repair eliminated every inequity” exceeds the sample evidence and design. Check individual task variation, comparable records and alternative explanations. A precise declaration cannot replace those inquiries.

check.question: What can the practice before-and-after observation establish?
check.correct: The recorded result changed after the repair, while attribution, comparability and remaining barriers need appropriate evidence.
wrong: A revised notice proves every person could use the process.
No further inquiry is needed because the average improved.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement recognizes the recorded change and preserves the separate questions about cause and full access.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Timing alone does not establish attribution or universal access. An improved average may hide variation and other changed conditions. Report the action, result and limits, then identify a suitable responsible review.

items.text: Both practice offices now use the same document names.
The revised notice includes the handoff explanation.
Recorded responses increased, with other conditions needing review.
Check whether the revised handoff works for the intended task.
One repair fulfills every equity-policy duty.
The average increase proves every barrier is eliminated.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to trace a connected task, test a possible barrier and review a supported response with appropriate responsibility.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Responses increased after the notice changed, and the team wants to claim the repair caused every result and eliminated all inequities.
options: Describe the action and recorded result, limits, alternative conditions and next responsible review.
Make the causal claim more technical without more evidence.
Hide the result because attribution is uncertain.
responses: The record can communicate useful progress without overstating cause or scope.
More technical wording cannot supply the missing comparison or evidence.
A bounded result remains useful when uncertainty is explained.

lessons.transfer: Write a review plan with implementation evidence, a task result, an alternative explanation, authority and next inquiry.

move.control: You can describe a supported result and appropriate follow-through.
move.failure: An outcome observed after a repair becomes a universal causal or compliance claim.
move.next: Use the practice sequence or a suitable draft to plan an evidence-based review.

jobAid.subtitle: Trace the task, investigate a possible barrier and plan a supported response.
remember: Linked steps can create a burden that an isolated instruction review misses.
A plausible mechanism or group difference is not a complete causal explanation.
A proposal and a learning exercise do not authorize rule changes or certify all responsibilities.

sections.heading: Map and inquire
items: Name the starting point, task boundary, steps and handoffs.
Separate documented steps from the expected path.
Describe a possible mechanism and evidence that would support or challenge it.

sections.heading: Check evidence
items: Match the measure to the task and intended result.
Check definitions, periods, denominators, missing information and authorized use.
Avoid cause, motive or individual-experience claims unsupported by the evidence.

sections.heading: Compare responses
items: Identify authority, applicable requirements and resources.
Trace benefits, new burdens and the full handoff for each option.
Record how affected input informed a changed or unchanged choice and its reasons.

sections.heading: Follow through
items: Check implementation separately from outcome and causal impact.
State the result, context and limits honestly.
Use actual required procedures and assign an appropriate next review.
